subject: Pharmacology
stem: A client on a continuous IV heparin infusion has an aPTT result of 110 seconds (control 30 seconds; therapeutic range 46–70). The client's platelet count has dropped from 250,000 to 90,000/mm3 over 48 hours. Which action should the nurse take FIRST?

options.text: Stop the heparin infusion and notify the provider
options.feedback: Correct. A >50% platelet drop with supratherapeutic aPTT suggests heparin-induced thrombocytopenia; heparin must be discontinued immediately.

options.text: Decrease the infusion rate per the titration protocol and recheck aPTT in 6 hours
options.feedback: Incorrect. Simply lowering the rate does not address the suspected HIT signalled by the platelet fall.

options.text: Administer protamine sulfate at the calculated reversal dose
options.feedback: Incorrect. Protamine is not first-line here and requires an order; stopping the drug and notifying come first.

options.text: Continue the infusion and transfuse one unit of platelets
options.feedback: Incorrect. Platelet transfusion in HIT can worsen thrombosis and does not correct the cause.

rationale: A precipitous platelet drop during heparin therapy signals possible HIT; the nurse stops heparin and notifies the provider before other measures.

subject: Pharmacology
stem: A client receives IV gentamicin every 8 hours. The morning trough level drawn just before the scheduled dose is 2.8 mcg/mL (therapeutic trough <2 mcg/mL). Serum creatinine has risen from 0.9 to 1.6 mg/dL. Which action is the priority?

options.text: Hold the dose and notify the provider of the elevated trough and rising creatinine
options.feedback: Correct. A high trough with rising creatinine indicates drug accumulation and nephrotoxicity risk; the dose is held and the provider notified.

options.text: Administer the dose now and draw a peak level 30 minutes after
options.feedback: Incorrect. Giving another dose when the trough is elevated compounds nephrotoxicity.

options.text: Administer the dose over a longer infusion time to reduce toxicity
options.feedback: Incorrect. Slower infusion does not lower an already-elevated trough or protect the kidneys.

options.text: Encourage oral fluids and reassess the trough with the next scheduled dose
options.feedback: Incorrect. This delays action while accumulation continues.

rationale: An elevated aminoglycoside trough with rising creatinine signals accumulation and nephrotoxicity; the nurse holds the dose and notifies the provider.

subject: Pharmacology
stem: Fifteen minutes into an IV vancomycin infusion, a client develops flushing and an erythematous rash over the face, neck, and upper torso with mild pruritus. Vital signs are stable. Which is the most appropriate nursing action?

options.text: Slow the infusion rate and continue monitoring; this is an infusion-related reaction
options.feedback: Correct. Flushing of the upper body from rapid vancomycin infusion (vancomycin flushing reaction) is rate-related; slowing the infusion typically resolves it.

options.text: Stop the drug permanently and document a true vancomycin allergy
options.feedback: Incorrect. This histamine-mediated reaction is not an IgE allergy and does not contraindicate future use.

options.text: Administer IM epinephrine for anaphylaxis
options.feedback: Incorrect. Stable vitals and isolated upper-body flushing do not indicate anaphylaxis.

options.text: Increase the infusion rate to finish the dose quickly and remove the drug
options.feedback: Incorrect. A faster rate worsens the histamine release.

rationale: Vancomycin flushing reaction is caused by rapid infusion and is managed by slowing the rate, not by stopping the drug or treating for anaphylaxis.

subject: Pharmacology
stem: A postoperative client receiving IV morphine via PCA has a respiratory rate of 6/min, is difficult to arouse, and has an SpO2 of 84%. Naloxone is prescribed. Which administration approach is most appropriate?

options.text: Administer small titrated IV doses of naloxone while monitoring respiratory rate
options.feedback: Correct. In an opioid-dependent postoperative client, naloxone is titrated in small increments to restore ventilation without precipitating severe withdrawal and uncontrolled pain.

options.text: Give the full ampule of naloxone as a rapid IV push to fully reverse the opioid
options.feedback: Incorrect. A large rapid dose can trigger acute withdrawal, severe pain, hypertension, and pulmonary edema.

options.text: Withhold naloxone and simply stop the PCA, then reassess in 30 minutes
options.feedback: Incorrect. With RR 6 and SpO2 84%, waiting is unsafe; reversal is indicated.

options.text: Administer naloxone subcutaneously and delay reassessment until it is absorbed
options.feedback: Incorrect. In an emergency with hypoventilation, the IV titrated route provides rapid, controllable reversal.

rationale: Naloxone is titrated in small IV increments in opioid-tolerant clients to reverse respiratory depression while avoiding acute withdrawal.

subject: Pharmacology
stem: A client stabilized on lithium presents with coarse hand tremor, ataxia, slurred speech, and vomiting. The client recently started a new medication. Which newly added drug most likely precipitated these findings?

options.text: Hydrochlorothiazide
options.feedback: Correct. Thiazide diuretics reduce renal lithium clearance and raise serum lithium, precipitating toxicity (tremor, ataxia, dysarthria, vomiting).

options.text: Acetaminophen
options.feedback: Incorrect. Acetaminophen does not significantly alter lithium levels.

options.text: Loratadine
options.feedback: Incorrect. This antihistamine does not affect lithium excretion.

options.text: Docusate sodium
options.feedback: Incorrect. A stool softener has no meaningful interaction with lithium.

rationale: Thiazide diuretics decrease renal lithium clearance, raising levels into the toxic range and producing neurologic and GI toxicity.

subject: Pharmacology
stem: A client receives a morning dose of NPH insulin at 0700 and regular insulin at 0700 before breakfast. At which time is the client at greatest risk for hypoglycemia from the NPH component?

options.text: Between 1500 and 1900 (late afternoon)
options.feedback: Correct. NPH peaks roughly 4–12 hours after administration, so a 0700 dose places peak hypoglycemia risk in the mid-to-late afternoon.

options.text: Between 0715 and 0745
options.feedback: Incorrect. That reflects the very early onset window, not NPH's peak.

options.text: Between 0900 and 1100 (mid-morning)
options.feedback: Incorrect. This is closer to the regular insulin peak, not NPH.

options.text: Between 0300 and 0500 the next morning
options.feedback: Incorrect. That window is beyond NPH's duration for a morning dose.

rationale: NPH is an intermediate-acting insulin peaking about 4–12 hours after dosing, placing greatest hypoglycemia risk in the afternoon for a morning dose.

subject: Pharmacology
stem: A provider prescribes a dopamine infusion at 5 mcg/kg/min for a client weighing 80 kg. The bag contains 400 mg of dopamine in 250 mL of D5W. At what rate (mL/hr) should the nurse set the infusion pump? Round to the nearest whole number.

options.text: 15 mL/hr
options.feedback: Correct. 5 mcg × 80 kg = 400 mcg/min = 24,000 mcg/hr = 24 mg/hr. Concentration = 400 mg/250 mL = 1.6 mg/mL. 24 ÷ 1.6 = 15 mL/hr.

options.text: 24 mL/hr
options.feedback: Incorrect. This is the mg/hr dose, not the volumetric rate after dividing by concentration.

options.text: 9 mL/hr
options.feedback: Incorrect. This underestimates by using an incorrect weight or concentration step.

options.text: 30 mL/hr
options.feedback: Incorrect. This doubles the correct rate.

rationale: Dose = 5 mcg/kg/min × 80 kg = 24 mg/hr; dividing by the 1.6 mg/mL concentration gives 15 mL/hr.

subject: Pharmacology
stem: Thirty minutes into a packed red blood cell transfusion, a client develops fever, chills, flank pain, and reports a sense of impending doom; urine appears dark. Which action should the nurse take FIRST?

options.text: Stop the transfusion and keep the IV line open with normal saline via new tubing
options.feedback: Correct. These findings suggest an acute hemolytic reaction; stopping the blood immediately and maintaining IV access with saline protects renal perfusion and is the first action.

options.text: Slow the transfusion rate and administer an antipyretic
options.feedback: Incorrect. Signs of hemolysis require stopping the transfusion, not slowing it.

options.text: Notify the blood bank and complete the reaction paperwork before intervening
options.feedback: Incorrect. Documentation follows stopping the transfusion and stabilizing the client.

options.text: Administer diphenhydramine and resume the transfusion once symptoms ease
options.feedback: Incorrect. Antihistamines treat mild allergic reactions, not hemolysis; the unit must not be resumed.

rationale: Fever, flank pain, dark urine, and doom indicate acute hemolytic transfusion reaction; the nurse stops the blood first and maintains saline through fresh tubing.

subject: Pharmacology
stem: While a nurse changes the cap on a client's central venous catheter, the client suddenly becomes dyspneic, anxious, and hypotensive with a churning murmur auscultated over the precordium. Which position should the nurse place the client in FIRST?

options.text: Left lateral Trendelenburg (left side down, head lowered)
options.feedback: Correct. Suspected air embolism is managed by positioning left side down with head lowered to trap air in the right ventricle apex, away from the pulmonary outflow tract.

options.text: High Fowler's position
options.feedback: Incorrect. Upright positioning can worsen air migration into the pulmonary circulation.

options.text: Right lateral with head elevated
options.feedback: Incorrect. Right side down promotes air passage into the pulmonary artery.

options.text: Supine with legs elevated only
options.feedback: Incorrect. Leg elevation alone does not trap air in the right ventricle.

rationale: For suspected venous air embolism from a central line, left lateral Trendelenburg traps air in the right ventricle and reduces pulmonary outflow obstruction.

subject: Pharmacology
stem: A client's total parenteral nutrition (TPN) bag runs empty and the next bag will be delayed 3 hours because the pharmacy is compounding it. Which nursing action best prevents the most immediate complication?

options.text: Hang 10% dextrose in water at the same rate until the TPN is available
options.feedback: Correct. Abruptly stopping high-dextrose TPN can cause rebound hypoglycemia; infusing dextrose maintains the glucose supply until the new bag arrives.

options.text: Flush the central line with heparin and leave it capped until the next bag
options.feedback: Incorrect. Capping the line risks rebound hypoglycemia from the sudden loss of dextrose.

options.text: Increase the rate of the maintenance normal saline line to keep the vein open
options.feedback: Incorrect. Saline provides no glucose and does not prevent hypoglycemia.

options.text: Administer the client's scheduled subcutaneous insulin as ordered
options.feedback: Incorrect. Giving insulin without dextrose would deepen hypoglycemia.

rationale: Interrupting high-dextrose TPN risks rebound hypoglycemia, so a dextrose-containing solution is infused at the same rate until the next bag is ready.

subject: Pharmacology
stem: A nurse is about to administer the first dose of lisinopril to a client newly admitted with hypertension. Which laboratory value most warrants holding the drug and contacting the provider?

options.text: Serum potassium 5.9 mEq/L
options.feedback: Correct. ACE inhibitors reduce aldosterone and cause potassium retention; giving lisinopril with a potassium of 5.9 mEq/L risks dangerous hyperkalemia.

options.text: Serum sodium 138 mEq/L
options.feedback: Incorrect. This sodium is within normal limits.

options.text: Fasting glucose 105 mg/dL
options.feedback: Incorrect. This value does not contraindicate an ACE inhibitor.

options.text: Hemoglobin 13.2 g/dL
options.feedback: Incorrect. This hemoglobin is normal and unrelated to ACE-inhibitor safety.

rationale: ACE inhibitors promote potassium retention, so a pre-dose potassium of 5.9 mEq/L should be reported before administration to avoid worsening hyperkalemia.

subject: Pharmacology
stem: A nurse reviews the record of a client discharged on warfarin. Which findings require follow-up before the client leaves? Select all that apply.

options.text: The client started an over-the-counter regimen of high-dose vitamin E and fish oil
options.feedback: Correct. These supplements increase bleeding risk and can alter warfarin effect.

options.text: The client's INR today is 5.2 with reported gum bleeding
options.feedback: Correct. A supratherapeutic INR with bleeding needs intervention before discharge.

options.text: The client plans to greatly increase intake of dark leafy greens for a new diet
options.feedback: Correct. Large swings in vitamin K intake destabilize INR and warrant counseling.

options.text: The client was newly prescribed trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole for a UTI
options.feedback: Correct. This antibiotic potentiates warfarin and raises INR.

options.text: The client takes the warfarin dose at the same time each evening
options.feedback: Incorrect. Consistent timing is appropriate practice.

options.text: The client wears a medical-alert bracelet noting anticoagulation
options.feedback: Incorrect. This is a recommended safety measure.

rationale: Bleeding-risk supplements, a supratherapeutic INR with bleeding, major vitamin-K diet changes, and interacting antibiotics all require follow-up on warfarin.

subject: Pharmacology
stem: A nurse cares for a client receiving cytotoxic chemotherapy with an absolute neutrophil count of 400/mm3. Which interventions are appropriate? Select all that apply.

options.text: Place the client in protective (neutropenic) precautions
options.feedback: Correct. An ANC of 400 indicates severe neutropenia requiring protective precautions.

options.text: Wear chemotherapy-rated gloves and gown when handling the client's body fluids for 48 hours
options.feedback: Correct. Cytotoxic drugs are excreted in body fluids; hazardous-drug PPE is used.

options.text: Avoid fresh flowers and uncooked fruits and vegetables in the room
options.feedback: Correct. These carry microbial risk for the neutropenic client.

options.text: Assess temperature and report a single reading of 38.0°C promptly
options.feedback: Correct. Neutropenic fever is an emergency; even a low-grade fever is reported.

options.text: Administer scheduled aspirin for mild discomfort
options.feedback: Incorrect. Aspirin increases bleeding risk and masks fever; it is avoided.

options.text: Take a rectal temperature for accuracy
options.feedback: Incorrect. Rectal measurement risks mucosal injury and infection in neutropenia.

rationale: Severe neutropenia demands protective precautions, low-microbial-risk environment, hazardous-drug PPE, and prompt fever reporting, while avoiding aspirin and rectal temperatures.

subject: Pharmacology
stem: A client taking a selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor was recently started on tramadol. Which findings would lead the nurse to suspect serotonin syndrome? Select all that apply.

options.text: Hyperthermia
options.feedback: Correct. Hyperthermia is a hallmark of serotonin syndrome.

options.text: Agitation and confusion
options.feedback: Correct. Altered mental status reflects serotonergic excess.

options.text: Myoclonus and hyperreflexia
options.feedback: Correct. Neuromuscular hyperactivity is characteristic.

options.text: Diaphoresis
options.feedback: Correct. Autonomic instability includes profuse sweating.

options.text: Bradycardia and hypothermia
options.feedback: Incorrect. Serotonin syndrome typically causes tachycardia and hyperthermia.

options.text: Flaccid paralysis with absent reflexes
options.feedback: Incorrect. Reflexes are increased, not absent, in serotonin syndrome.

rationale: Serotonin syndrome presents with hyperthermia, altered mentation, neuromuscular hyperactivity (myoclonus, hyperreflexia), and autonomic signs such as diaphoresis.

subject: Pharmacology
stem: A nurse prepares to administer IV potassium chloride to a client with a potassium of 2.8 mEq/L. Which principles guide safe administration? Select all that apply.

options.text: Never administer potassium chloride by IV push
options.feedback: Correct. IV push potassium can cause fatal cardiac arrest and is prohibited.

options.text: Use only premixed diluted solutions and an infusion pump
options.feedback: Correct. Premixed, pump-controlled infusion prevents inadvertent bolus.

options.text: Verify adequate urine output before and during the infusion
options.feedback: Correct. Potassium is renally excreted; oliguria risks hyperkalemia.

options.text: Assess the IV site for infiltration and phlebitis during infusion
options.feedback: Correct. Potassium is irritating to veins and can cause phlebitis or tissue injury.

options.text: Administer the ordered dose as a rapid bolus to correct the level quickly
options.feedback: Incorrect. Rapid administration is dangerous and can be fatal.

options.text: Withhold cardiac monitoring since the level is only mildly low
options.feedback: Incorrect. Continuous or frequent monitoring is important during potassium replacement.

rationale: Safe IV potassium requires dilution, pump control, no IV push, confirmed urine output, and site and cardiac monitoring.

subject: Pharmacology
stem: A client receives a continuous IV aminophylline infusion titrated to a serum theophylline level. Which findings suggest theophylline toxicity requiring the nurse to reassess the titration? Select all that apply.

options.text: Tachycardia with new premature ventricular contractions
options.feedback: Correct. Cardiac dysrhythmias are a toxicity sign.

options.text: Persistent nausea and vomiting
options.feedback: Correct. GI upset is an early toxicity indicator.

options.text: Restlessness and tremor
options.feedback: Correct. CNS stimulation reflects rising levels.

options.text: A serum theophylline level of 26 mcg/mL
options.feedback: Correct. Levels above roughly 20 mcg/mL are toxic.

options.text: A serum theophylline level of 12 mcg/mL
options.feedback: Incorrect. This is within the therapeutic range.

options.text: Resolution of wheezing with improved air movement
options.feedback: Incorrect. This is a therapeutic response, not toxicity.

rationale: Theophylline toxicity presents with dysrhythmias, GI upset, CNS stimulation, and serum levels above about 20 mcg/mL.

subject: Pharmacology
stem: A nurse is about to give the morning dose of digoxin to a client with heart failure. Which 3 findings should prompt the nurse to hold the dose and notify the provider?

options.text: Apical heart rate of 52 beats per minute
options.feedback: Correct. An apical rate below 60 warrants holding digoxin.

options.text: Serum potassium of 2.9 mEq/L
options.feedback: Correct. Hypokalemia potentiates digoxin toxicity.

options.text: Serum digoxin level of 2.4 ng/mL
options.feedback: Correct. This exceeds the therapeutic range (0.5–2.0 ng/mL).

options.text: Blood pressure of 128/78 mmHg
options.feedback: Incorrect. This is a normal blood pressure.

options.text: Apical heart rate of 76 beats per minute
options.feedback: Incorrect. This rate is acceptable for administration.

options.text: Serum potassium of 4.2 mEq/L
options.feedback: Incorrect. This is a normal potassium level.

rationale: Digoxin is held for bradycardia below 60, hypokalemia, and supratherapeutic digoxin levels, all of which increase toxicity risk.

subject: Pharmacology
stem: Protamine sulfate is the appropriate reversal agent for a client with a supratherapeutic INR caused by warfarin who is actively bleeding.
rationale: Protamine reverses heparin; warfarin-related bleeding is reversed with vitamin K and, for urgent reversal, prothrombin complex concentrate or fresh frozen plasma.

subject: Pharmacology
stem: For each medication, click the correct antidote or reversal agent.
rationale: Vitamin K reverses warfarin, flumazenil reverses benzodiazepines, and N-acetylcysteine treats acetaminophen toxicity.

subject: Pharmacology
stem: For each medication, select all adverse effects the nurse should monitor for (each drug may have more than one).
rationale: Loop and aminoglycoside agents cause ototoxicity; ACE inhibitors cause hyperkalemia and dry cough; potassium-sparing diuretics cause hyperkalemia.

subject: Pharmacology
stem: A client with diabetic ketoacidosis is on an IV insulin infusion. The nurse anticipates adding {1} to the IV fluids once the serum glucose reaches about 200 mg/dL, and will closely monitor for {2} during the infusion.
rationale: Dextrose is added as glucose falls to prevent hypoglycemia while ketoacidosis clears, and insulin drives potassium intracellularly, risking hypokalemia.

subject: Pharmacology
stem: A nurse reviews a client 1 hour after IV hydromorphone. Findings: client is [[unarousable to sternal rub]], respiratory rate [[5 breaths per minute]], [[pinpoint pupils]], SpO2 [[82% on room air]], blood pressure [[118/70]], temperature [[37.1°C]]. Highlight the findings that indicate opioid toxicity requiring immediate intervention.

chunks.feedback: Correct. Profound sedation is a sign of opioid toxicity.
Correct. Severe respiratory depression requires immediate action.
Correct. Miosis is a classic opioid effect.
Incorrect. This blood pressure is normal.

rationale: Opioid toxicity is recognized by depressed consciousness, bradypnea, miosis, and hypoxemia; normal blood pressure and temperature are not the concerning cues.

subject: Pharmacology
stem: A laboring client on an IV magnesium sulfate infusion for preeclampsia becomes lethargic with slurred speech. Complete the diagram by selecting the condition, actions to take, and parameters to monitor.

tokens.text: Administer an additional bolus of magnesium

rationale: Lethargy and slurred speech signal magnesium toxicity; the nurse stops the infusion, prepares calcium gluconate, and monitors reflexes and respirations.

subject: Pharmacology
stem: A client develops laryngeal stridor, wheezing, and hypotension immediately after an IV antibiotic dose. Place the nurse's actions in the correct priority order.
tokens: Apply high-flow oxygen and maintain the airway
Give ordered IV fluids and antihistamine
Document the reaction and update the allergy record
